chief_complaint: fluctuating confusion, lethargy, and right-sided weakness 4 weeks after minor head bump against car door
hpi_details: 82M on chronic anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation brought by family due to 1-week history of fluctuating mental status, lethargy, slurred speech, and progressive weakness in right arm and leg. concerns: family worried because he sleeps 18 hours a day and cannot feed himself with right hand
expectations: wants urgent brain CT scan and reversal of blood thinners if bleeding is found
pmh: Atrial Fibrillation, Hypertension, Chronic Kidney Disease Stage 3
medications: Apixaban 5mg BID, Metoprolol 25mg BID, Lisinopril 10mg daily

clinical_knowledge.topic: Chronic Subdural Hematoma evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Chronic Subdural Hematoma is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Hold Apixaban immediately, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: fluctuating confusion, lethargy, and right-sided weakness 4 weeks after minor head bump against car door

Key HPI features: 82M on chronic anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation brought by family due to 1-week history of fluctuating mental status, lethargy, slurred speech, and progressive weakness in right arm and leg. Family recalls patient bumped his head against the car door frame 4 weeks ago without immediate symptoms or loss of consciousness.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: HR 74 (irregularly irregular), BP 146/82. GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6). Mild right facial droop, right upper extremity pronator drift, 3/5 motor strength in right arm and leg. Non-contrast head CT reveals a large crescent-shaped (concavoconvex) hypodense-to-isodense extra-axial fluid collection over the left cerebral convexity measuring 1.8 cm thickness with 9 mm rightward midline shift and effacement of left lateral ventricle.
Relevant background/PMH: Atrial Fibrillation, Hypertension, Chronic Kidney Disease Stage 3
Current medications: Apixaban 5mg BID, Metoprolol 25mg BID, Lisinopril 10mg daily
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Chronic Subdural Hematoma.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Acute ischemic stroke without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as anticoagulant use with head trauma, which warrants urgent evaluation; reversal is indicated for clinically significant intracranial bleeding.
management_principles: Administer Andexanet alfa (or 4-factor Prothrombin Complex Concentrate - 4F-PCC if Andexanet unavailable) to reverse Factor Xa inhibition
Urgent neurosurgery consultation for left burr hole drainage or twist-drill craniostomy with closed drainage catheter placement to evacuate chronic subdural fluid under local/general anesthesia
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 82M on direct oral anticoagulation presenting with subacute fluctuating encephalopathy and focal hemiparesis 4 weeks post-minor head trauma.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: HR 74 (irregularly irregular), BP 146/82. GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6). Mild right facial droop, right upper extremity pronator drift, 3/5 motor strength in right arm and leg. Non-contrast head CT reveals a large crescent-shaped (concavoconvex) hypodense-to-isodense extra-axial fluid collection over the left cerebral convexity measuring 1.8 cm thickness with 9 mm rightward midline shift and effacement of left lateral ventricle.
reference_soap.assessment: Symptomatic Left Chronic Subdural Hematoma (cSDH) with mass effect and midline shift in anticoagulated elderly patient.
reference_soap.plan: Hold Apixaban immediately. Administer Andexanet alfa (or 4-factor Prothrombin Complex Concentrate - 4F-PCC if Andexanet unavailable) to reverse Factor Xa inhibition. Urgent neurosurgery consultation for left burr hole drainage or twist-drill craniostomy with closed drainage catheter placement to evacuate chronic subdural fluid under local/general anesthesia.

learning_objectives: Recognize typical clinical presentation of chronic subdural hematoma in elderly anticoagulated patients following minor or remote head trauma
Differentiate crescent-shaped (concavoconvex) subdural hematoma morphology from biconvex epidural hematoma on head CT
Understand emergency reversal protocols for direct oral anticoagulants (Factor Xa inhibitors via Andexanet alfa or 4F-PCC) prior to surgical intervention
Describe surgical evacuation techniques via burr hole drainage and middle meningeal artery embolization

teaching.one_liner: A slow venous bleed under the skull, often from a trivial head bump weeks earlier in an elderly patient on blood thinners, causing gradually worsening confusion and one-sided weakness; clinically significant bleeding requires anticoagulant reversal before surgery.
red_flags: Anticoagulant use with head trauma warrants urgent evaluation; reversal is indicated for clinically significant intracranial bleeding

must_ask.say: Did he bump his head at any point in the past month?
Is he taking a blood thinner for his heart rhythm?
How has his mental status and weakness changed, and does it fluctuate?
How much sleeping and how much help does he need now?

history.answer: My father has been drifting in and out of confusion for the past week, and his right side has become increasingly weak.
Before this week, his mind was sharp and he lived independently, managing his daily routines and finances without any memory issues.
It started gradually about a week ago, and it fluctuates; some hours he seems almost normal, but other times he gets very confused and sleepy.
He has become terribly sluggish and now sleeps nearly eighteen hours a day, taking several seconds to answer simple questions, though he hasn't seen any hallucinations.
About four weeks ago, he bumped his head against the car door frame while getting in, but he didn't lose consciousness or have any cuts, so we didn't think much of it.
Yes, he takes apixaban twice every day because he has an irregular heartbeat.
Over the past few days, his right arm and leg have gotten weak to the point where he cannot hold a spoon, and his words sound noticeably slurred.
Yes, his smile looks uneven and the right corner of his mouth has been drooping slightly since yesterday.
He mentioned having a dull, nagging head ache over the past few days, but he hasn't had any nausea or vomiting.
No, he hasn't had any shaking episodes, convulsions, staring spells, or loss of bladder control.
No, he has had no fever, chills, cough, or changes in how his urine looks or smells.
No, his neck moves freely without any stiffness, and bright lights do not bother him.
He does not have diabetes, and his blood sugar has always been normal whenever it was checked.
He has been drinking fluids, but eating has been tough because of his arm weakness; he hasn't had any diarrhea or vomiting.
No, all his prescriptions have remained exactly the same for years, and he uses a daily pill organizer so he hasn't missed or doubled any doses.
He does not drink alcohol at all, and all his pill bottles are accounted for with no chance of an overdose.
He eats a balanced diet and hasn't lost weight, and he hasn't complained of any double vision.
No, nobody else at home is sick, and we do not use gas heaters or have any chemical exposures.
He has moderate chronic kidney disease, but he has never had liver trouble, jaundice, or abdominal swelling.
No, he has never had any psychiatric illness or episodes like this in the past.
We are terrified that he suffered a stroke or is rapidly developing severe dementia, especially since he cannot use his right hand.
We want him to get an urgent brain scan right away, and if there is any bleeding, we hope his blood thinners can be reversed.
He has a history of atrial fibrillation, high blood pressure, and stage 3 chronic kidney disease.
He had an appendectomy when he was a young man, but no other surgeries or hospitalizations.
He takes apixaban 5 milligrams twice daily, metoprolol 25 milligrams twice daily, and lisinopril 10 milligrams once daily.
He has no known allergies to any medications or foods.
He is a retired postal worker, lives with my mother and me, and has never smoked cigarettes.
His father passed away from heart disease in his late seventies, and his mother lived into her nineties without any neurological disorders.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 146/82 mmHg, heart rate is 74 beats per minute and irregularly irregular, respiratory rate is 16 breaths per minute, temperature is 36.7 °C, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air.
Elderly male lying in bed, noticeably lethargic but easily arousable to voice, appearing mildly confused.
Glasgow Coma Scale score is 13 (eye opening 3, verbal response 4, motor response 6); he knows his name but is disoriented to date and location with reduced attention span.
Pupils are equal, round, and reactive to light at 3 mm bilaterally; extraocular movements are full without nystagmus.
Mild right-sided lower facial droop with slurred speech; forehead wrinkling is preserved and tongue protrudes midline.
Motor strength is 3 out of 5 in the right arm and right leg, with noticeable right arm pronator drift, while the left side is intact at 5 out of 5.
Brisk 3+ deep tendon reflexes in the right arm and leg compared to 2+ on the left, with an extensor plantar response (Babinski sign) on the right.
No neck stiffness; Kernig and Brudzinski signs are both negative.
Faint, resolving yellowish contusion over the left temporal scalp without open laceration, step-off deformity, or acute swelling; no tongue bite marks.
Heart rhythm is irregularly irregular with normal S1 and S2; no murmurs, rubs, or gallops heard.
Breath sounds are clear bilaterally with good air movement and no crackles, wheezes, or rhonchi.
